📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The only points path to nonstop business class service to French Polynesia.

Picture this: you're reclining in a fully flat bed somewhere over the Pacific, a glass of Champagne in hand, watching the sun melt into the ocean from 35,000 feet. In eight hours, you'll land in Papeete — French Polynesia's gateway to overwater bungalows, turquoise lagoons, and the kind of trip people save their whole lives for. And you got here on points. This is the Air France business class seat to Tahiti, and it represents one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. Not just because of where you're going — though Tahiti is bucket-list by definition — but because of the staggering gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you'll pay in miles. **The math will genuinely stop you in your tracks.** A business class ticket from Los Angeles (LAX) to Papeete (PPT) on Air France regularly retails between **$5,000 and $12,000 per person**. That's the cash reality. But with Flying Blue miles — Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program — you can book the same seat for as few as **88,000 miles**. At the high end of retail pricing, that's a value of **13.6 cents per point (CPP)**. Even at the low end, you're extracting **5.7 CPP** from miles that most programs value at 1–2 cents. In the ChooseFI community, we talk constantly about optimizing every dollar toward financial independence — and a redemption that turns 88,000 transferable points into a $5,000–$12,000 experience is about as powerful as it gets. Here's what makes this feel different from your average business class booking: Air France operates a **Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner** on this route, featuring a modern, premium business class cabin with direct aisle access for every seat, noise-reducing windows, better humidity levels, and that unmistakably French touch in service and catering. You're not just flying in a recliner — you're flying in a genuine lie-flat pod on one of aviation's most celebrated aircraft. And this is the only nonstop option. Air France is the **sole carrier operating nonstop LAX–PPT** service. That's not a coincidence — it's a pricing inefficiency baked into the route's geography, and it's exactly the kind of structural advantage the ChooseFI community knows how to exploit.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program is the only way to book the only nonstop flight between Los Angeles and Tahiti using points — and that program happens to offer some of the most generous award pricing in the world.

According to recent reports, flying Blue uses a dynamic award pricing model, meaning costs fluctuate based on demand and availability. That sounds like a disadvantage — and sometimes it is. But here's the inefficiency: Flying Blue releases Promo Rewards every single month. These are fixed-price award seats on select routes, discounted 25–50% off standard award pricing. When Tahiti appears as a Promo Reward destination (which it does periodically), the pricing drops dramatically — and crucially, Promo Reward tickets eliminate carrier-imposed fuel surcharges entirely.

Fuel surcharges on Air France-operated flights are normally moderate, but they're real — they can add $200–$500 to an award ticket. Promo Rewards wipe those out. This is the pricing inefficiency: Flying Blue is essentially subsidizing this cabin to drive demand, and you can capture the subsidy.

Recent findings suggest that here's the beautiful part for ChooseFI members: virtually every major transferable points currency sends to Flying Blue at a 1:1 ratio. That means:.

According to recent reports, the Chase, Amex, and Citi transfers are instant, which matters enormously when you're racing to lock down a business class award seat before someone else grabs it. You find the seat, you confirm it's available, then you transfer — because once points leave your bank, they don't come back.

This is the single most notable rule in booking award travel, and it's especially critical here. Flying Blue's award availability on the LAX–PPT route is genuinely limited — this is a popular route to a popular destination on a single aircraft. You do not transfer points speculatively. You find confirmed availability on flyingblue.com, verify the seat count and pricing, then immediately transfer from your Chase, Amex, or Citi account (all instant) and book.

In a recent development, flying Blue allows open-jaw routing, meaning you could potentially fly into Papeete and out of another South Pacific destination if Air France serves it — giving sophisticated travelers a way to build a multi-destination itinerary without paying for a separate return trip to your origin city. It's a small but meaningful piece of flexibility in a program that doesn't always offer it.

On the first of each month, Flying Blue releases its upcoming Promo Rewards. These are fixed-price, reduced-cost awards with no fuel surcharges. That's a car payment for most families. Even if it's in the travel budget, it's a brutal number to justify when you're pursuing financial independence.

It has been revealed that the points price: 88,000 Flying Blue miles per person, round-trip in business class. The CPP math: At $8,000 in cash value against 88,000 miles, you're extracting 9.1 cents per point — nearly 5–9x the baseline value of transferable points currencies. That's the ChooseFI lens: every point you've earned on everyday spending just multiplied in purchasing power.

#159818. The Ultimate Life Coach

📅 18 May 2024 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2081 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

The Ultimate Life Coach

📅 18 May 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.
  • You’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises.
  • But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.

You’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises. And then to put thousands of hours into everything else I value as well: family, health, friends, adventures, building stuff, and even writing the occasional blog post. No complaints about any of this.

But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.

According to recent reports, to most people, this sounds like a dream come true. Especially if you combine total freedom with plenty of money, life is just a non-stop blissful playground of self actualization, right?

Well, maybe, but maybe not. In reality, the answer depends on who you are.

Freedom and money reveal a person’s true strengths and weaknesses, and the result is a spectrum with “Unlimited drugs and booze on the couch” at one end, and “Create and manage a series of nonprofit foundations which employ thousands of people to research and invest in medical advances and clean energy” at the other.

For most of my journey so far, I seem to have found the balance pretty naturally. My Dad job was very intense for the first decade, but somehow I also had time to build and restore quite a few houses in the neighborhood, take plenty of intense trips to interesting places, give some talks and make some videos, and still write a few hundred blog posts.

But in these last few years, I have started slowing down, and it has become more and more difficult to wrangle and focus myself to get these things to happen as often.

Instead of constantly bouncing around the construction site building cool things, or falling into laser focus on the keyboard finishing an article that I just had to share with you, I found myself retiring to the couch earlier and earlier each afternoon, seeking distraction on the phone and wishing I had the energy and focus to do those other more enjoyable things.

Sources indicate that so I fought back, by learning more about health and wellness. Trying to study and train my way into more energy and focus and motivation. And you’ve seen some of the results here, in articles I’ve shared about daily habits, steering clear of excessive comfort, and more.

In a recent development, and all of these things really work, IF you take the knowledge and actually put it into action. And therein lies the problem:.

It has been revealed that I kept learning effective new things, and successfully incorporating them into my life. They would work for a while, but gradually my brain would invent various excuses to stop doing them consistently, leaving me with plenty of knowledge but far too little accomplishment to show for it.

Until finally, just a few months ago, I realized that I had been sabotaging my own progress by turning my biggest life advantage into a disadvantage:.

I have been using my freedom too much – in order to avoid doing things that I didn’t feel like doing.

It has been revealed that see, freedom is great if it frees you from leaving your children at 5am so you can drive an hour through a traffic jam to sit in an office building for nine hours. But that same freedom goes to waste if you then just plunk the kids down in front of a playlist of cheap cartoons while you lounge in the corner to scroll Facebook all day.

You need to use it to do things that are even more valuable than the job you just quit. And if you can’t do that, you might as well just keep the damned job.

This is what I was doing, while lying about it to myself. I would focus on the easy things which are still good for me, like taking care of the house or hanging out with friends who live nearby. But I avoid doing the harder things – which for me means the things that require more planning, energy or focus. Even though these are the things that allow me to lead the life I enjoy most.

Recent findings suggest that let’s use workouts as an easy example. I already know that on a minute-for-minute basis, this is the single most effective thing almost anybody can do with their time because it drastically improves every other area of life. But despite knowing this, I was still following this pattern:.

“I want to get in a really good weight training workout today.But I don’t feel like doing a workout because it’s hard.So I’ll try to grease the wheels for myself so it’s easier to achieve. I’ll pick the perfect time of day when the weather is nice, and my energy level is high. I’ll set up my gym in advance the night before.And when that golden moment of perfect conditions hits,I’ll hit the gym!“.

According to recent reports, but between you and me, that moment didn’t always come. Some weeks I’d achieve it 2-3 times, some weeks I’d get “busy” and make excuses like “well at least I walked a lot today”. Some days I would complete a great workout, but when recording it in the journal I’d see that the previous one was over a week ago.

And the results of this lackluster effort were exactly what you’d expect: lackluster fitness.

Sources indicate that then something changed and I learned that there’s a much better way to get those workouts done. It’s by replacing the long, meandering, frankly wussypants dialog above with this one:.

Recent findings suggest that I want to work out today.I don’t feel like it.^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

I’m using workouts as an example because this is the behavior I managed to change most successfully, but the exact same technique applies to everything else that you or I want to do, but fail to do regularly.

The key is learning to watch over yourself like an Eagle and identify that exact moment of hesitation.

And then instead of using it as a trigger for excuses, you use it as a trigger for action.

Recent findings suggest that it’s so counterintuitive at first, but then obvious in retrospect. Hesitance feels shitty in the moment, and it really can ruin your life if you listen to it too often. But the ultimate solution is usually to run directly towards, rather than away from, the stuff you don’t want to do.

So really, Hesitation can be the ultimate life coach.

Using Extremely Badass People as Fuel.

Sources indicate that as part of writing this article, I shared the idea around with friends to test it out first. And I was initially surprised to get mixed results. About half of them could relate with me: they felt they were underachieving in life and wanted to do more. The other half though I was crazy: these people feel they are already doing too much, raising multiple kids and managing multiple businesses and training for ironman triathlons in the mountains.

It has been revealed that the overachievers go through life nicely buzzed but often stressed. When hearing them describe their schedules, I was absolutely not envious. At the same time, they weren’t impressed with my schedule either because it’s too easy. We could both benefit from making adjustments towards the center.

Impressive overachiever friends are one thing, but the thing that really flipped the switch for me was hearing a podcast interview with our planet’s most extreme example of driving yourself beyond your former limits, David Goggins.

According to recent reports, I learned about his life story with a mix of awe and horror. Severely beaten as a child, he grew up with a looming wall of psychological demons and concerns, but his reaction was the unique part: he has been driven to compulsively seek out and overcome extreme hardship, not just to unimaginable levels but hundreds of times beyond that.

From pushing through several near-death experiences just to qualify for a Navy SEALS career, to breaking his own legs, heart and lungs from the constant exertion of things like running 240 miles over four days without sleeping, to setting a world record of 4025 bar pull ups over 24 hours (shredding his hands to look like ground beef in the process), the man does things I would never have thought are even close to possible for a human.

And that flipped a switch for me, by putting my own incredibly easy, under-achieving life into perspective.

Because while I absolutely do not want any part of the Goggins life, and I would gladly live my life never having run more than 10 miles at a single stretch, I do find it incredibly helpful to learn that pretty much all of our barriers are entirely mental, not physical or placed upon us by the outside world.

Industry observers note that sure, we do have different starting points and different amounts of luck. But instead of thinking of life like this:.

I now realize that things are more like this:.

And that’s a really empowering way to think about life, that feels like the sky has opened way up.

So the podcast was just an introduction. I wrote down the particularly concise quote “You already fuckin’ know what to do.” on a piece of cardstock, stuck it to my bathroom mirror, and started acting on it immediately.

Suddenly, I was able to hit the gym every single day because I had two ways to approach it: wanting to put in a workout, and not wanting to put in a workout, either of which became a trigger to work out immediately.

Recent findings suggest that and of course, once I finally put in the effort, it started working. Even though I’ve been sorta into this type of training since I was a teenager, I have mostly floated along on a plateau for years. But with this change in attitude, I gained ten pounds of lean weight over the first four months, returning to the strength and flexibility that I had at age 25, and every single joint in my body feels like it has been upgraded to a study, well oiled spring.

I also used the “catch yourself at the moment of hesitance” trick to get myself to run instead of walk more often (over 20 runs since I got back to Colorado last month), get over to the MMM-HQ coworking space for more work and socializing visits, and even to sit back down at the computer to write this post for you. While I’ve found that too much blogger work (and internet “success”) is a bad thing, there is still a right level that works for me. But it takes a lot of discipline to be willing to do it, because of all the other easier and more thrilling activities I could be doing with this same stretch of time.

According to recent reports, for me, fully internalizing this one powerful piece of inspiring profanity has been transformative. But I still find that returning regularly to the well makes all this work even better. So I downloaded both of the Goggins audiobooks and worked through them in little chunks on my morning walks over the period of a month. Then I moved on to Peter Attia’s Outlive, and Jocko Willink’s Extreme Ownership.

It has been revealed that while the intellectuals fret about the perils of “Bro Science” or the “Toxic Masculinity” of today’s tribe of health podcasters and question their motivation, I simply absorb the messages that work for me and discard the rest. Find people who make you reach a little higher, and feed on their energy.

And for me, being exposed to successful, strong, athletic people who squeeze a lot of work out of themselves is a big source of inspiration. It helps me do more with my day, which is exactly what works for me right now at this phase of life.

And I wish you more of what works for you too!

Picture this: you walk into a stunning hotel lobby — maybe it's the Hyatt Regency Kyoto, maybe it's the Andaz Maui at Wailea, maybe it's a chic Hyatt Centric in the heart of a city you've always wanted to explore. You hand over your World of Hyatt card at check-in, and the night is on the house. Not because you're a high roller. Not because you spent $50,000 on a credit card. Because you crossed a spending threshold you were hitting anyway, and Hyatt rewarded you with a free night certificate that covers any Category 1–4 property in the entire portfolio. This is what the ChooseFI community means when we talk about travel rewards done right: identifying the moments where a credit card benefit perfectly intersects with your normal life, and extracting maximum value with minimum complexity. ## The Math That Makes This a No-Brainer Here's the value proposition in plain numbers. Category 4 Hyatt properties — places like the Thompson Nashville, the Hyatt Regency Maui, or the Andaz San Diego — regularly command **$200 to $400 per night** in cash. On peak dates, holiday weekends, or in premium markets, that number climbs even higher. Your free night certificate covers any of these properties at no additional points cost. None. Zero. This isn't a discount. It's a full, unrestricted free night at properties that charge real-world luxury rates. Why does this represent a genuine pricing inefficiency? Because Hyatt's Category 1–4 certificates are earned through a flat spending threshold — $15,000 on the World of Hyatt Credit Card in a calendar year — and can be redeemed at properties whose nightly rates vary enormously. A Category 4 certificate costs the same to earn whether you use it at a $150 roadside property or a $400 resort. The system rewards you for targeting the high end of the range every single time. For a household already putting everyday spending on a rewards card, $15,000 across a full calendar year is often an achievable benchmark. Groceries, utilities, insurance premiums, quarterly tax payments — it adds up faster than you think. And when it does, Hyatt drops a certificate in your account that can deliver **$300–$400 in hotel value** without spending a single additional point. In the World of Hyatt program — consistently rated the **best hotel loyalty program for value per point** — this certificate is one of the most quietly powerful perks on any hotel card in the market.

According to recent reports, the core mechanism here isn't a transfer partnership exploit or a routing rule loophole. It's simpler and more durable than that: Hyatt's Category system creates a ceiling, not a floor. When you earn a Category 1–4 free night certificate, you're not locked into a $150-a-night budget motel. You're handed a key that opens any door in that range — and some of those doors lead to genuinely spectacular properties.

It has been revealed that hyatt operates on a fixed award chart, ranging from 3,500 points for a Category 1 night all the way up to 45,000 points for a Category 8 night. Unlike programs that use dynamic pricing (where award costs swing with cash demand), Hyatt's chart is static. A Category 4 property costs the same 15,000 points whether it's a Tuesday in February or New Year's Eve.

According to recent reports, your free night certificate functions exactly like those 15,000 points — but you earned it through card spending, not through a points balance. This means the certificate has a defined and predictable value: whatever a Category 4 property charges in cash on the night you use it is exactly what you're getting for free.

In a recent development, the pricing inefficiency exists because Hyatt assigns categories based on average nightly rates across the year — but peak-season rates at desirable Category 4 properties can blow well past that average. A Hyatt Regency in a major city might be Category 4 because its average annual rate qualifies, but on a conference weekend or holiday weekend, that same room might cost $350–$400. Your certificate captures that peak-season value without any upcharge.

If you want to stack a certificate with a separate points redemption — say, booking multiple nights where the first is covered by the certificate and subsequent nights use transferred points — you have two strong, flexible on-ramps into the Hyatt ecosystem. Chase Ultimate Rewards is the workhorse of the FI community's travel rewards stack, and having Hyatt as an instant 1:1 partner makes it one of the most actionable transfer relationships in the game.

Sources indicate that hyatt charges no fuel surcharges on award redemptions — a meaningful distinction compared to some airline programs where surcharges can swallow most of your savings. Your certificate redemption is clean: one certificate, one free night, no surprise fees at checkout beyond standard resort fees (which, to be fair, do apply at some properties — more on that in Pro Tips).

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. As a World of Hyatt Credit Card holder, your card activity will naturally keep your account active, so expiry is rarely a concern for cardholders. But if you ever cancel the card, make sure you use your points and certificates before they age out.

Booking a World of Hyatt free night certificate is genuinely one of the easiest processes in all of travel rewards. Here's the complete walkthrough from certificate to check-in.

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search function. You can filter by World of Hyatt category — specifically, search for Category 4 properties in any destination you're targeting. Don't shortchange yourself by defaulting to a Category 1 or 2 property out of habit. The certificate works at any Category 1–4 property, so always target the top of the range. Look for properties with high nightly cash rates — this is where your certificate delivers the most value.

Once you've identified a target property, search your dates on hyatt.com and switch the search to "Use Points." Category 4 properties will show award availability for 15,000 points per night. If award availability highlights for that date, your certificate will cover it. Hyatt's booking window opens 395 days in advance, so for peak travel dates — holidays, major events, popular travel seasons — you can and should book the maximum window out.

Proceed through the booking process. At the payment step, you'll see an option to "Apply Free Night Award" or select your certificate from your account. Select the Category 1–4 certificate. The system will apply it and your total cash charge drops to $0 for the room rate (plus taxes and any applicable resort fees).

Industry observers note that hyatt operates on a fixed category system where each property is assigned a category from 1 to 8 based on the brand and location, not the current market rate. This creates a structural pricing inefficiency: a Category 4 property in a high-demand market like Maui or Kyoto charges the same certificate cost as a Category 4 in a mid-tier city. Your free night certificate works at all of them equally. Unlike hotel programs with dynamic pricing where the cost of a free night fluctuates with demand, Hyatt's fixed chart means you can target the highest-value Category 4 properties without paying more. Sources indicate that this sweet spot is built for the everyday FI household that's already spending $15,000 or more annually on a single credit card and wants to redirect that activity toward a meaningful travel benefit. ## Rated: Easy (4/5 Beginner Friendly) This is one of the most accessible sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem, and that's by design. The certificate mechanism removes the two biggest friction points in traditional points redemptions: **finding the right number of points** and **navigating complex transfer timing**. You earn the certificate passively through spending, it posts to your account automatically, and the booking process on hyatt.com is as intuitive as booking any other hotel stay. ## What Makes It Easy - **No transfer required** — the certificate lives in your World of Hyatt account, ready to apply at checkout - **Fixed pricing** — Category 4 is Category 4 everywhere in the world; no dynamic pricing surprises - **Simple availability search** — hyatt.com's award search is clean and straightforward ## The One Genuine Challenge: Availability at Popular Properties The only real friction point is award inventory at high-demand Category 4 properties on desirable dates. Hyatt limits how many award rooms it releases per night, and popular properties in destinations like Hawaii or New York fill rapidly. **Three ways to beat this:** 1. #159789. $656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

📅 24 Jul 2024 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1995 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

$656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

📅 24 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.
  • Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”.
  • When I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I used to read Mr. Money Mustache”,.

“Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.

Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”.

When I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh. Because on the one hand, when you put a bunch of personal life details online like this, being misunderstood is just part of the package. But on the other hand, if the critics could peek in and see our real lives – not just mine but those of all the Mustachians – they would have to give up their conspiracy theories and accept the fact that this stuff just works.

Sources indicate that because really, not much has changed when it comes to the basics. Like many MMM readers over the past twelve years, my total wealth level has increased pretty regularly. But also like many of us, I haven’t felt the need to change very much about my spending because I was doing my best to live an enjoyable life in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that how have so many people found such great success? I think we Mustachians have something that’s a bit more rare and special than standard financial advice, which is what makes it work so well:.

Standard Advice: Slash your spending and make sacrifices until you reach a certain savings percentage, and beyond that it doesn’t matter, it’s all personal choice. More income? Great, that means you don’t have to sacrifice as much! FatFIRE for everyone!

Mustachianism: Cultivate a love of efficiency, creativity, self awareness, and self improvement. Use this knowledge to improve your life in all ways, including those which help you live better even as your monthly expense rate drops over time.

So what does this mean in practice?

In a recent development, well, I’ll give you some examples from my own present-day life. Things I do because I happen to enjoy them, which also happen to save a lot of money. Some of these are normal, some are silly and may end up in some future gossip magazine hit piece, but all of them happen to work for me, so the critics can be damned.

As I list each item, I’ll include an estimate of how much the activity saves me per decade, because you should always think at least in terms of decades. To make that calculation yourself, just use the “rule of 172” – take a monthly expense and multiply it by 172 to estimate how much it would compound into over ten years, if invested.

1) Fixing my own House (and everybody else’s too).

Recent findings suggest that I’m a major believer in self-sufficiency, and working to build up the skills to manage the most key parts of your own life without depending on too many things (or people) that are outside of your control. In other words, one giant recipe for a happy life is simply to Become a Producer of the Things You Most Enjoy Consuming.

In a recent development, and in my case, I happen to love houses. I like living in beautiful, functional spaces and sharing them with friends. But most houses are ugly and poorly designed when you buy them, so I realized that I also love solving problems and redesigning old buildings to become new again. I enjoy this process so much that I spend most of my free time doing it – on both my own properties and the homes of friends.

In a recent development, and I love teaching other people to gain power over their own houses too. It’s amazing how great people feel as they lose their fear and dependence on outside contractors, and gain the ability to fix and maintain things with their own two hands.

Savings: An average of $20,000 per year = $287,000 per decade.

You know what’s great? Having so much money that you can buy whatever you want – high quality things which get delivered to your front door the very next day.

It has been revealed that you know what’s even better? Not buying some of those upcoming things, and instead finding ways to share, repurpose and buy equally high quality items from other people who don’t need them any more. All while building up your own community and creating new friendships in the process.

It has been revealed that craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and even NextDoor all have Buy Nothing groups for most areas. In the MMM-HQ community, we run a Discord server with about 200 local people, who chat around the clock on a wide range of subjects. They help each other with major projects in one channel called #diyhowto, and give away and sell things on #forsale and #buynothing.

Although our private Discord group is my favorite, I also use Craigslist regularly, and probably save (and earn) a few thousand every year thanks to the habit:.

Savings: About $42,000 per decade.

We all know that Mr. Money Mustache’s biggest contribution to personal finance is to insist that bike transportation is the best way to get around. And I still feel this way. As we learned in The True Cost of Commuting, cars cost at least 50 cents per mile to operate, while bikes are much cheaper, mainly due to reduced depreciation and maintenance costs (which are even bigger than the gas savings).

It has been revealed that I do still use bikes (or walking) for at least 95% of my local trips these days, but because I live in the center of a small city, my life is pretty local. So this still only adds up to about 2000 miles per year, a savings of “only” $14,000 per decade.

In a recent development, but when you choose active transportation, there’s much more to the picture than just cutting your car expenses. You’re changing everything about your physical and mental health picture for the better, which brings us to the next point of….

Recent findings suggest that although I’m no competitive athlete, whenever I see an option to make my body work a bit harder, I usually take it. Stairs instead of elevators, running the golf course instead of using a golf cart, moving my own furniture and appliances instead of calling a mover, shoveling snow and raking leaves instead of using a machine.

When I face a decision like this, I simply ask myself the question: “Well, Mustache. Do you want MORE health and fitness, or LESS?” Putting it in that context makes the answer obvious. Every bit helps, because when it comes to your body, the rule is pretty much use it or lose it.

But how much money does this save? There’s no real way to calculate it exactly, but I like to think of it this way: The US average health care spending is about $13,000 per person per year. My lifetime costs due to illness or medication so far have been just about zero, plus I know I’ve had more energy and greater productivity due to being healthy. Let’s just put it very conservatively and set the estimated savings and benefits at $10k per year which means.

Estimated Savings:  $140,000 per decade.

5) Saving Energy by Running my home like a Glamping Retreat.

Here’s where things get a bit silly, but my level of joy is actually at its greatest.

My personality type is probably a weird combination of an engineer, a carpenter, an artsy hippie, and a mad scientist. Oh, and a devoted homebody too. Because of this, my favorite activity most days is to just run around my house taking care of things and trying new little experiments and improvements.

Sometimes I’ll cut a few big holes on on the South side of the house and install sliding doors and big windows to allow nice sunbeams and passive solar energy to get into my house and give me free heat in the winters. Other times it’s just smaller things to save energy and live more at at one with the seasons of my area:.

Recent findings suggest that even taken all together, these things are pretty small – the average combined gas and electric bill for my area is about $250 per month, while my usage adds up to about $75. So while we’re only saving about $30,000 per decade for what sounds like a lot of work to most people, I consider this to be the biggest win because I enjoy living in “MMM’s Energy Efficiency Playground” so much.

6) Local Living over Constant Travel.

“Hey, we’re having a big back yard pool party next weekend to celebrate Amy’s graduation from kindergarten, can you make it?”.

According to recent reports, “OH NOOOO!!! We will be off in at Disneyland that whole week! We planned the trip months ago, I wish we could make it!

It has been revealed that as I type this in the height of the summer season, I really feel this effect at its fullest: almost all of my friends are off on trips, and my guest suite here at home is almost constantly full. People are traveling a lot, and many of them sound like they wish they could spend a few more of their precious summer weeks and weekends at home.

In a recent development, I’ll let you in on a little secret: you can! The trick is saying, “no thanks” more often to intends that involve you being away, and “yes please” to things that let you stay at home. The benefits are numerous:.

It has been revealed that estimated Savings: Even if you replace just two weeks of travel for a family of four, with equivalent time at home you might save $5,000 per year in direct costs and a further $5,000 per year in incidental benefits like the health and local friendships. This would work out to a shocking $143,000 per decade of wealth increase!

Industry observers note that of course, travel is generally a good thing for broadening the life experience of you and your kids. It’s worth spending on, lavishly at times. But the key is to balance it out and be discerning, keeping the most enriching trips and pruning a few off the bottom of the list. And remembering that home time is valuable and healthy too.

According to recent reports, and Whoa! We’ve already built up a huge list and I feel like I was just getting started.

Taken all together, we’ve already detailed things that compound to $656,000 every decade, which already more than double the median wealth that most American seniors have as they cruise nervously into their retirement years – after over 40 years of work!

It has been revealed that and now that I’ve been writing this blog for over ten years myself, I can safely say that over $656,000 of even my most recent worth increases are directly attributable to these simple habits. The same ones many of us have been enjoying and preaching about all along, both before and after our retirement dates.

If money is in genuinely short supply, you could go a lot further than the examples in this article. And indeed, there’s a lot more laid out in this blog or the MMM Boot Camp email series.

But one of the points of Mustachianism is that you usually don’t have to try all that hard. Just tweaking your lifestyle to be slightly less ridiculous and more efficient than average is usually all it takes.

In a recent development, in the comments: what are your quirks and frugal indulgences? The things you do now to save money, or things you still do even after it’s no longer about the money? I often wonder how widespread this frugality-just-for-fun is. But since we Humans are a naturally curious and problem solving species in our natural state, I suspect there are many more of us out there.

World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings.

Fuel Surcharges via Partner Programs.

Industry observers note that picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific. The door closes. A flight attendant in a crisp JAL uniform offers you a warm towel and asks how you'd like your appetizer served. The flat bed is already made with a proper duvet. Outside the window, the sun is setting over the ocean. You're nine hours into a 12-hour flight to Tokyo, and you feel more rested than you did when you boarded. This is JAL's Sky Suite — one of the most celebrated business class products in the world — and with the right travel rewards strategy, your family can experience it for a fraction of what everyone else is paying. Here's the math that stops people cold: a round-trip business class ticket from San Francisco to Tokyo on JAL typically retails for **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's not a typo. Premium transcontinental fares are genuinely that expensive, and most people simply accept that they'll never sit up front on a 12-hour flight across the Pacific. But the ChooseFI community knows better. That same seat — the same flat bed, the same Champagne, the same Sky Suite cocoon — is available for **60,000 miles** when booked through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. At a retail value of $5,000 to $10,000, you're looking at **8.3 to 16.7 cents per point** in value. For context, most travel rewards experts consider anything above 1.5 cents per point a good redemption. This one can be up to *eleven times* that benchmark. The pricing inefficiency exists because partner award programs — like Alaska and American — use fixed award charts that were negotiated years ago, before JAL's hard product became one of the most sought-after cabins in the sky. JAL hasn't raised these partner pricing levels proportionally as cash fares have climbed. The gap between what you pay in points and what the market charges in dollars is enormous, and it's yours to exploit right now. This isn't a loophole that's about to close tomorrow. It's a structural feature of the loyalty system — one that rewards people who understand how to use their points strategically rather than burning them on domestic economy upgrades. For anyone on the path to financial independence, where every dollar and every point is treated with intention, this is exactly the kind of asymmetric opportunity worth understanding.

In a recent development, the core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award. This is the aha moment that separates casual points customers from strategic ones.

JAL operates its own loyalty program — JAL Mileage Bank — but it charges significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often running $100 to $500 or more per ticket. When you book JAL business class through JAL Mileage Bank itself, those surcharges erode a substantial portion of your points value before you even leave the ground. The ChooseFI community's editorial guidance here is unambiguous: book JAL through partner programs to avoid this tax on your redemption.

There are two primary programs where you can book JAL business class at 60,000 miles round-trip on the transpacific route:.

Alaska Mileage Plan prices JAL business class at 60,000 miles for a round-trip between North America and Japan. Alaska is a oneworld partner of JAL and honors JAL's genuinely strong award availability. Critically, Alaska does not pass through JAL's fuel surcharges to awards booked through Mileage Plan. This is a massive advantage.

Sources indicate that american AAdvantage also prices the same route at 60,000 miles round-trip. Both programs use fixed award charts, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash fares do — a $10,000 ticket at peak cherry blossom season costs exactly the same points as a ticket in a slower travel month.

Sources indicate that neither Alaska Mileage Strategy nor American AAdvantage is a direct transfer partner from the major US bank programs in the same way Chase or Amex partners work. However, you have real pathways:.

For Alaska and American miles specifically, the strongest earning strategies involve:.

It has been revealed that both Alaska and American use fixed award charts — meaning the price in miles is the same regardless of how high the cash price climbs. This is the structural inefficiency at work. A seat that retails for $10,000 during peak season still costs 60,000 miles. The chart doesn't care about demand; it just prices by region and cabin. As long as JAL releases availability — and they do — the gap between cash cost and points cost remains enormous.

JAL also allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award, which means you can potentially add a stop in Tokyo itself while continuing to another Japanese city, or fly into one city and out of another — all at no additional miles cost.

This is the cardinal rule of all travel rewards bookings: never transfer points until you have confirmed availability. Points transfers are generally irreversible.

This is the same structural mismatch that creates sweet spots throughout the oneworld alliance — the booking program's pricing does not match the operating airline's product quality.

A quick search on Google Flights or JAL's own website for this route in business class will typically show cash prices ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 per person — let's use $7,000 as a reasonable midpoint for this example. For two people, you're looking at a $14,000 cash outlay before you even think about hotels in Tokyo.

Booked through Alaska Mileage Plan: 60,000 Alaska miles per person, round-trip. For two travelers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles total, plus taxes and fees (which Alaska keeps minimal for JAL awards, typically under $100 for the pair).

The CPP math: $7,000 in value ÷ 60,000 miles = 11.7 cents per point — squarely in the middle of the 8.3-to-16.7-cent range and nearly 8 times what most people get burning points on domestic economy tickets.

On the 777-300ER, you may get the Apex Suite — a staggered configuration with direct aisle access from every seat and a similarly flat, private sleeping environment.

In a recent development, during the quarter, markets contended with the first Federal Reserve rate hike since 2023, stubborn inflation, higher oil prices, and ongoing geopolitical tensions. Against this backdrop, U.S. equities delivered mixed results. July saw investors rotate away from high-momentum AI and technology stocks followed by a two-month period when these same stocks recovered. Market leadership narrowed sharply toward large-cap technology and AI-linked names, driving large-cap growth indexes to end the period slightly higher while small-cap and mid-cap growth indexes ended lower.

Industry observers note that baron Asset Fund (the Fund) declined 6.22% (Institutional Shares) in the third quarter, performing similarly to the Russell Midcap Growth Index (the Index), which fell 5.84%. The quarter marked a sharp reversal of the market conditions that predominated during the first half of the year. The so-called âAI winnersâ cohort that had powered the Index higher in recent quarters, including semiconductor, data center, and power companies, sold off. Software and other higher-quality, lower-beta businesses led amid heightened market volatility.

In a recent development, according to MSCIâs Barra factor attribution, style factors were a substantial tailwind to the Fundâs performance for the first time in several quarters. The Fundâs persistent underexposure to Momentum and Beta paid off as both factors reversed, and its larger-cap positioning within the mid-cap universe added further value. Many of the Fundâs software and services holdings also performed well, helping partly offset stock-specific weakness associated with the Fundâs large position in rocket, satellite, and spacecraft manufacturer Space Exploration Technologies Corp (SPCX). (SpaceX).

From a sector perspective, Industrials contributed approximately 170 basis points of relative gains, driven by strong stock selection and lower exposure to this lagging sector. Notable declines in.

aerospace & defense and construction & engineering stocks pressured the Indexâs Industrials. The Fundâs Industrials holdings held up better, thanks largely to double-digit gains from financial software and services provider SS&C Technologies (SSNC) Holdings, Inc. and defense and government consulting firm Booz Allen Hamilton Holding Corporation (BAH). Both companies delivered solid fundamental results and benefited from the broader rebound in software, information services, and consulting stocks as concerns about AI disruption eased.

Solid stock selection in Health Care and Real Estate also added value, led by life science tools manufacturer Mettler-Toledo International Inc (MTD). and senior housing REIT Welltower Inc (WELL). As discussed below, Mettler-Toledoâs stock performed well as a result of strong second quarter results and a raised full-year outlook. Welltower posted modest gains during the quarter despite a challenging backdrop in which most real estate securities declined, extending its strong performance from the first half of the year. The organization continued to execute well, delivering robust cash flow growth driven by strong occupancy gains, healthy rent growth, and ongoing margin expansion, all of which reflect powerful demographic tailwinds supporting demand for senior housing.

The Fund also benefited from being overexposed to Financials, one of the better performing sectors in the Index, as well as its lack of or lower exposure to the lagging Consumer Discretionary and Utilities sectors. Together, these contributed nearly 150 basis points of relative gains. In addition, several of the Fund's holdings that had sold off meaningfully earlier in the year based on fears of AI-driven business model disruption staged partial recoveries. These included syndicated research provider Gartner (IT), Inc., application software vendors Guidewire Software (GWRE), Inc. and Veeva Systems Inc (VEEV)., and financial data and analytics firm FactSet Research Systems Inc (FDS).

Industry observers note that partly offsetting these gains was the Fund's overexposure to the lagging Communication Services sector through its sizable position in SpaceX, which detracted approximately 160 basis points from relative performance. As discussed below, we remain confident in SpaceX's long-term prospects. Underexposure to Information Technology (IT) and Energy, two of the best performing sectors in the Index, also proved costly, detracting more than 170 basis points from relative results.

In last quarter's letter, we discussed how multiple contraction across the software and services group was the main driver of recent underperformance, overshadowing improving business fundamentals. That shifted in the September quarter, as the Fund's software and services stocks rebounded after a period of disappointing performance. The group, which includes Veeva, Gartner, Procore Technologies (PCOR), Inc., SS&C, FactSet, Samsara Inc (IOT)., and Guidewire, appreciated by double digits and contributed more than 200 basis points, driven by a combination of accelerating growth and multiple expansion.

Industry observers note that the Fund nonetheless declined for the quarter because of weakness in the Other group. SpaceX's pullback, along with multiple contraction among many of the Fund's AI infrastructure and power beneficiaries, including Forgent Power Solutions, Inc., Vertiv Holdings Co (VRT), Cerebras Systems Inc., Quanta Services (PWR), Inc., and Amphenol Corporation (APH), weighed on performance. Encouragingly, these losses stemmed from multiple compression rather than fundamental issues.

In a recent development, we believe that shares of syndicated research provider Gartner, Inc. rallied as investors began to appreciate the valuation disconnect in beaten down information services stocks. We believe that the growth rate of Gartner's contract value is poised to reaccelerate as the company enhances its product offerings, retrain its sales force, and benefits from easier comparisons in its public sector end market. We also view Gartner as an underappreciated beneficiary of AI, as organizations increasingly seek guidance from trusted third-parties in navigating the risks and opportunities presented by AI technologies. In addition, we expect the company's earnings and free cash flow to grow meaningfully faster than its revenue as Gartner expands margins and returns excess capital through share repurchases. Management is on pace to deploy nearly $2 billion of free cash flow toward share repurchases this year, which we estimate could reduce the company's share count by roughly 15% to 20%.

Mettler-Toledo International Inc. is a leading provider of precision instruments and services used in research and development, quality control, and manufacturing processes across the life sciences, food, and chemicals industries. The stock contributed to performance following strong second-quarter results and a raised full-year outlook. Local-currency sales grew 6%, exceeding prior guidance of 3%, supported by better-than-expected growth in China and strength across other emerging markets. Earnings per share also exceeded sell-side estimates. In addition, positive commentary on business trends from life sciences tools peers, including Thermo Fisher Scientific (TMO) and Agilent, contributed to Mettler-Toledo's share price appreciation. We think the company is well positioned to benefit from several positive trends, including life sciences investment in China and new U.S. plant construction by biopharmaceutical companies. Over the long term, we believe Mettler-Toledo should generate mid-teens or better annual earnings-per-share (EPS) growth.

According to recent reports, shares of property and casualty insurance software vendor Guidewire Software, Inc. rallied as investors began to appreciate the valuation disconnect in beaten down software stocks. Guidewire's InsuranceSuite platform serves as the core system of record for insurance carriers, functioning as the single source of truth for policies, claims, premiums, and payments. Given the complexity, highly regulated nature, and digital format of insurance policies, we believe this system is particularly critical and valuable. We think the core-system opportunity alone represents nearly $20 billion of annual recurring revenue (ARR). In our view, AI will meaningfully expand this opportunity by enabling automation and intelligence on top of the organization's existing platform. Guidewire is already bringing fresh AI-enabled capabilities to market and signing customers, and we expect adoption to accelerate over the coming year. Finally, we expect Guidewire to benefit from AI-driven productivity gains, which should help the company grow faster while reducing its operating costs.

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. develops and launches advanced rockets, satellites, and spacecraft, with the long-term goal of making humanity multi-planetary. The stock detracted from performance as shares pulled back from highs reached after its initial public offering, despite strong underlying business fundamentals. We remain long-term shareholders and believe the manufacturer is in the early stages of a multi-decade growth opportunity. SpaceX's first results as a public company reinforced our conviction, with revenue nearly doubling year-over-year and losses narrowing sharply on high incremental margins. Growth was driven by rapidly scaling, multibillion-dollar compute-hosting deals with AI leaders, including Anthropic and Google (GOOGL), alongside momentum in its Starlink Internet connectivity business. Management guided to a robust $100 billion annualized revenue run rate by year-end 2026 and up to five times more compute exiting 2027, well above Street expectations. SpaceX also closed its acquisition of Cursor, a premier enterprise AI-powered coding platform, accelerated product development with Grok Bot and more advanced Grok models, and progressed toward full reusability of its Starship rocket.

Industry observers note that vertiv Holdings Co is a global leader in critical digital infrastructure for data centers, including electrical and thermal management equipment and related services. Shares declined as second quarter organic growth came in slightly below guidance, even as management raised its full-year outlook, with broader weakness in AI infrastructure stocks adding pressure. Vertiv is benefiting from the industry's shift toward modular solutions to alleviate field labor shortages, thanks to its broad product portfolio and large field service team. The firm is also well positioned to support upcoming technology transitions, including liquid cooling and direct current architectures. We see meaningful long-term upside from strong organic growth, margin expansion, and complementary acquisitions, supported by a strong balance sheet.

Global hotelier Hyatt Hotels Corporation detracted from performance as investors grew concerned that higher oil prices, interest rates, and inflation could pressure consumers and travel budgets. Nevertheless, consumer spending remains resilient, particularly on travel and experiences. Hyatt continues to grow new units at a mid-single-digit rate, while revenue per available room is accelerating from low- to mid-single-digit growth. We expect these trends to support margin and cash flow expansion, generating capital to reinvest in the business, pursue accretive tuck-in acquisitions, and increase share repurchases. Hyatt's strong balance sheet provides additional flexibility to fund growth or to allocate more capital to share buybacks. The stock continues to trade at a significant discount to its public hotel peers despite a similar mix of attractive fee-for-service business. We believe this discount should narrow as investors see continued growth in the business.

In a recent development, as of September 30, 2026, the Fund held 50 positions. The Fund's 10 largest holdings represented 62.0% of net assets, and the 20 largest represented 76.7%. The Fund's largest weighting was in the Communication Services sector at 31.7% of net assets. This sector includes our investment in SpaceX. The Fund held 16.6% of its net assets in the IT sector, which includes application software companies, electronic components businesses, and IT consulting firms. The Fund held 14.5% of its net assets in the Industrials sector, which includes investments in research & consulting companies, construction and engineering firms, electrical components & equipment businesses, and aerospace & defense contractors. The Fund held 11.8% of its net assets in Health Care, which includes investments in life sciences tools & services companies and health care equipment businesses. The Fund also had significant weightings in Financials at 10.7% and Consumer Discretionary at 6.1%.

As the table above demonstrates, the Fund's largest investments have mostly been owned for significant periods, with 7 of the 10 largest holdings held for longer than a decade. This is consistent with our approach of investing for the long term in companies benefiting from secular growth trends with significant competitive advantages and best-in-class management teams.

We initiated a position in Rubrik, Inc., which provides cyber resilience software that backs up an organization's data and user identities and restores them swiftly and cleanly after a ransomware attack or breach. The firm's founding insight was that legacy backup products, built decades ago to recover from equipment failures and natural disasters, were poorly suited to an era in which attackers deliberately destroy or encrypt backup copies before demanding a ransom. Rubrik instead designed its platform on the assumption that breaches are inevitable. Its backup copies cannot be altered or deleted, and the platform continuously analyzes its history of changes to identify threats and the last uncompromised point to which a customer can safely return.

Rubrik's approach has enabled the company to steadily gain market share from incumbent software vendors. It now includes more than 40% of the Fortune 500 as customers and generates approximately $1.7 billion of subscription ARR, which is growing more than 30% a year.

According to recent reports, we believe the spread of AI makes Rubrik's platform more essential. Increasingly capable AI models are making cyberattacks cheaper, faster, and more sophisticated, compressing the time between intrusion and damage from months to minutes and elevating recovery to a board-level priority. AI is also multiplying the data that companies must protect and introducing a newly introduced class of risk. Autonomous AI agents can modify or delete corporate data at machine speed.

Rubrik's Agent Cloud product monitors these agents and can surgically reverse their harmful actions, and it has already won its first paying customers. The manufacturer has a strong record of turning new products into meaningful businesses, most recently identity recovery, which surpassed $50 million of ARR roughly a year after launch. More than half of ARR now comes from products beyond its original on-premise backup offering. With penetration still in the low teens among large enterprises and existing customers increasing their spending by roughly 20% a year, we see a long runway for growth. As the business scales, we estimate free cash flow margins to expand toward management's long-term target of 25% or more, which should bode well for the stock long term.

Charles River Laboratories International, Inc. is a leading provider of outsourced "pre-clinical" drug development services: the research models, toxicology studies, and quality-control testing that a therapeutic drug requires on its path toward human trials. About 60% of the organization's revenue comes from its Discovery and Safety Assessment (DSA) segment, which runs the GLP toxicology studies that regulators demand before a drug can enter clinical trials. Charles River holds roughly one-third of the outsourced in vivo safety assessment market, supports around 1,500 Investigational Upcoming Drug programs a year, and has worked on more than 80% of recent FDA-approved drugs.

Another roughly 20% of revenues are in its Research Models and Services segment, which breeds the mice and animals used in early-stage research. The remaining 20% or so is Manufacturing Solutions: endotoxin and microbial testing, as well as biologics lot-release testing. Both are written into validated manufacturing processes and regulatory filings, making it difficult for clients to switch vendors.

It has been revealed that charles River suffered nearly three years of organic revenue decline as biotechnology funding dried up, and this cycle is now turning. In its most recent quarter, Charles River posted its first organic growth since late 2023. The net book-to-bill ratio in its key DSA segment reached 1.19 times, the highest level in nearly four years. The pharmaceutical industry has long under-invested in its early-stage drug development pipeline, and Charles River is benefitting as that pipeline is replenished. Management has also simplified Charles River's portfolio, divesting assets to focus on its core business.

According to recent reports, management recently committed to a meaningful acceleration in Charles River's organic revenue growth of 5% to 7% through 2030, ongoing operating margin expansion, and low double-digit compounded EPS growth. We view these goals as achievable, and perhaps conservative. Management itself described their targets as having "no moonshots, " and they exclude any benefit from AI.

We believe that AI is more likely to prove a tailwind than a threat to Charles River's business. AI is emerging as a potentially transformative technology assisting in identifying potential candidates in the drug discovery process. We expect Charles River to remain integral to validating that expanding pipeline of potential new drugs. In June, Charles River became the partner for TuneLab, a platform Eli Lilly (LLY) built to allow other drug developers to use its AI models. Charles River's role is to run standardized animal safety testing for participating companies, generating the kind of clean, consistent data these models need to learn from. We believe that the largest constraint on drug research successfully integrating AI is data, not algorithms. We expect researchers to conduct additional experiments to supplement their own data, and this increased activity should be a multi-year tailwind of demand for Charles River's services.

According to recent reports, we continued to build our position in Edwards Lifesciences Corporation, a leading manufacturer of heart valve replacement and repair products. We discussed the firm in detail last quarter.

We reduced our position in Space Exploration Technologies Corp., which remains an outsized holding in the Fund. As discussed last quarter, we remain quite optimistic about the company's future prospects in multiple very large and growing markets, including rocket introduces, voice and internet connectivity through its Starlink satellite network, AI models, and space-based AI infrastructure. The Fund's shares in SpaceX are subject to a staggered lockup that extends through August 2027, and we intend to continue reducing our holdings over time. We also reduced our holdings in two stocks that have performed well in 2026, both beneficiaries of the massive ongoing investment into AI data centersâAmphenol Corporation, which makes various interconnect, sensor and antenna solutions, and Quanta Services, Inc., a specialty contractor focused on electrical generation and infrastructure. We exited positions in two companies that failed to meet our growth expectationsâcontact lens manufacturer The Cooper Companies, Inc. and online sports betting firm DraftKings Inc.

In a recent development, as discussed last quarter, recent Index returns have been disproportionately driven by a narrow group of stocks deemed to be long-term winners in an AI-driven transformation of the global economy. Many investors have been chasing stock momentum and intriguing stories without paying sufficient attention to these businesses' extended valuations and possible long-term competitive risks.

According to recent reports, in contrast, we believe that many of the Fund's holdingsâin areas including software, IT consulting, business services, real estate brokerage, insurance brokerage, and wealth managementâhave been improperly penalized. We believe that investors' concerns are overstated about looming AI-driven disruption to these companies' business models and profitability. We believe this sell-off has indiscriminately punished many high-quality, competitively advantaged businesses.

We are encouraged that several of these stocks performed better this quarter. Nevertheless, many still trade at or near historically low valuation levels, even though their ongoing financial results demonstrate these businesses' resilience. We remain optimistic that these strong resultsâand stock price appreciationâwill continue. We believe the market will continue to recognize that these companies are utilizing AI in ways that should continually improve their products, lower their cost structures and enhance, rather than undermine, their competitive positions.

Recent findings suggest that our Space Exploration Technologies Corp. investment exposes the Fund to the long-term growth of AI, as well as several other large, dynamic markets. The Fund expects to remain a significant investor in SpaceX. But, as the lockup on its holdings expires, the Fund will manage its position size. We will balance our enthusiasm for SpaceX's business prospects against the Fund's objective to remain appropriately diversified among securities and industry sectors, as well as its mid-cap growth investment mandate.

We remain frustrated by the absolute and relative performance of mid-cap growth stocks. The Russell Midcap Growth Index has dramatically underperformed the Russell 1000 Growth Index, the primary large-cap growth index, during the past decade, and the divergence between these indexes continues to become more pronounced. Over the past five years, for example, mid-cap growth has trailed large-cap growth by nearly 900 basis points annualized.

Based on rolling five-year returns for the two indexes, mid-cap growth's relative underperformance is right now at approximately the 99th percentile of historical results. We believe this period of nearly unprecedented underperformance is unlikely to persist, which makes this an attractive time to invest in fast-growing, competitively advantaged, well-managed mid-cap businesses.

Thank you for investing alongside me.

Momentum captures the tendency of stocks with strong recent price performance to continue outperforming, and of weak performers to continue lagging. Positive exposure indicates high short/mid-term momentum (good recent performance). Negative exposure indicates low short/mid-term momentum (poor recent performance). Beta explains common variation in stock returns due to different stock sensitivities to market or systematic risk that cannot be explained by the US Country factor. Positive exposure indicates high beta stock. Negative exposure indicates low beta stock. Earnings Per Share (EPS) is a commonly used measure of a organization's profitability. It indicates how much profit each outstanding share of common stock has earned. Free Cash Flow (FCF) represents the cash that a company generates after accounting for cash outflows to support operations and maintain its capital assets. Free Cash Flow (FCF) Margin is a measure of profitability for a business. FCF Margin takes the free cash flow that a business generates and compares it against the revenue they earned during the same period. Operating Margin is a company's profit for every dollar of sales after deducting production costs like wages and raw materials but before accounting for interest and taxes.

#159768. Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

📅 13 Oct 2024 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2007 w)
