General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Six Dumb Misconceptions About The Economy (that the Politicians Want You To Believe)

📅 13 Oct 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.
  • As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs.
  • But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Well, it looks like we’re here in another US election year already.

As Advanced Mustachians, we already know that the ongoing battle of Harris vs. Trump should not be consuming much of our time. Sure, we do our research and cast our votes but after that we move right on to focus on other things within our own circle of control.

But out of all the things the politicians like to bicker about, there’s one area where MMM does need to set the record straight, and that area is of course money. Your money, the economy in general, and the overall wealth of the nation.

In a recent development, politicians are already not known for being the sharpest tools in the shed when it comes to technical stuff like science, technology, or economics. But this year the discourse has become particularly dumb, as our candidates try to manipulate undecided voters in swing states with ideas that are based on irrational emotions rather than sound economic sense.

For one particularly funny example, you may have noticed that the competing party (Trump in this case) is attacking the incumbents (Biden/Harris) over the “bad economy.” When in fact the US economy is stronger than it has ever been, with the lowest unemployment we’ve ever seen as well.

It’s hard to imagine a better situation than we have right now, and in fact the recent bout of higher inflation is a sign that things have been going too well, and we needed to step on the brakes with the help of higher interest rates.

In a recent development, but somehow the people still seem to believe that we have a “bad” economy. Take a look at this Gallup poll showing that while most people (85%) are doing really well right now, they assume that it’s just their own good fortune – only 17% believe the economy is doing well.

This is mathematically impossible, because if most people are doing well, that’s the definition of a good economy! And suspiciously enough, this widespread wrongness correlates quite nicely with the rise of social media misinformation.

So the politicians and the news have been doing the opposite of what they should be doing in an ideal situation (sharing accurate information). And sure, we can always just ignore their speeches and go on with our lives. But when it comes to economics, knowledge is power (and money). The more accurately we understand how things really work, the wealthier we will all become.

So with all that in mind, I hereby present you with my list of the….

Top Dumb Things Politicians Want You To Believe About The Economy.

1: The President Controls the Economy.

If there’s a recession, the opposition party likes to blame it on the current president. If the economy is booming, the current president likes to give himself (or possibly soon herself) credit for all of that success. But really, the US economy is way too big – and thankfully way too free – for the president to control or really even influence all that strongly.

In reality, our economy is a gigantic machine which converts labor and materials into things like iPhones, hospitals and pumpkin pies. And although we’re the biggest economy at 26% of the planet, we are still heavily influenced by that much bigger 74% of economic activity that the other 7.6 billion people on Earth are busy producing everywhere else.

When we have our inevitable little boom and bust cycles, they are mostly caused by the normal cycle of irrational exuberance (and greed) like the 2007 housing boom, followed by brief periods of extreme fear and pessimism like the 2008-2012 financial and housing crash.

According to recent reports, the government does play a role too, by setting tax rates and other rules. But the effects of these policies are usually so delayed and unpredictable, that you can’t draw a straight line between today’s president and today’s economy. In other words, the government does its best to adjust the rudder on our giant ship, but in the short term our economy lurches around on the waves and storms of the ocean.

2: The President Controls Interest Rates.

It has been revealed that this one is especially funny to me, as our candidates feign sympathy for the hard life of middle class Americans, who now face higher borrowing costs on their credit cards and car loans and mortgages. They claim they will fight to bring the interest rates down. Trump even goes as far as bullying our Federal Reserve board members (who can only do their jobs if we allow them to function as independent experts) and suggesting that he would take over the whole department, if elected.

In a recent development, the real story is that while monetary policy would be a terrible tool to leave in the hands of a sitting president (see Argentina), it does function as an excellent set of gas and brake pedals for the economy if used properly. When things slow down and unemployment gets too high, a cut to the interest rates will produce a boost in everything from latest jobs to stock prices. But if things get too hot, you get rapid inflation which can mess up the system.

3: Inflation has Made Life Harder for Americans (and the President Can Magically Reverse it).

It has been revealed that this line of reasoning is even dumber than the last one. For a couple of years after the Covid era, we had rapid inflation. It was caused by a rare combination of a goods shortage caused by things like factory closures and remote work, plentiful demand from government stimulus spending and low interest rates. These factors have since ironed themselves out, and inflation is back down to an ultra-low 2.4%.

It has been revealed that but most significantly, wages have still risen faster than inflation so we are all better off than before! Since 2019, overall prices are up 19% and our wages are up 21%. So even after all that inflation, we are still doing just fine. But the candidates are still bickering over inflation as if it’s an actual problem, and even worse promising to “bring prices back down”. And they’ve managed to convince the electorate that “higher wages and prices” is the same thing as “a bad economy”. Which is just plain wrong.

Recent findings suggest that bonus dumbness: politicians also occasionally blame “greedy corporations” for increasing prices to hoard profits. While price increases are totally acceptable in a market system (as a business owner you are free to set prices wherever you like), in reality it doesn’t usually happen because our markets are too competitive. For example, a recent deep analysis from NPR demonstrated that no, grocery stores haven’t made any windfall profit at all off of this recent bout of Covid-fueled inflation.

4: The President Controls Housing Prices.

Sources indicate that one important thing that has changed over the past ten years is that US house prices and rents have both risen much faster than general inflation and even wages. On the positive side, interest rates have also risen which tends to make houses feel more expensive and is supposed to help bring house prices down. But it hasn’t happened yet which means we have the double whammy of higher prices and higher interest costs for mortgage borrowers.

The dumb part is that our candidates are proposing things that would make the problem even worse, like subsidies for first-time homebuyers or schemes to reduce the interest rates. When really the solution is to increase the supply of housing, which I personally think will happen if we stop putting up roadblocks for homebuilders (myself included) to build housing.

Things like faster and cheaper permits, less onerous and expensive building codes, eliminating suburban-style zoning and setback and car parking rules, and changing laws so that NIMBYs no longer get any say over what other people do with their own land could all help reduce the cost of building a house by about 50%, rapidly and permanently.

5: The President Controls Gas Prices, and They Are At the moment “High” and We Want Them Lower.

It has been revealed that ahh, gasoline! The most ridiculous of things to worry about and the fuel for many of MMM’s rants since 2011.

First of all, on an inflation-adjusted basis, gasoline is still about the same price as it was in 1950: in the $3-4 range per gallon, in today’s dollars.

Recent findings suggest that secondly, it is so cheap that even with our huge inefficient American vehicles, the average household is still only spending 2.5% of their disposable income on the stuff! (The funny part is that they spend many times more on the rest of the car ownership experience while thinking gas is the part that is expensive).

Industry observers note that third, gasoline has been obsolete for almost a decade now. You can get a used electric car for less than the price of a comparable used gas car, or if you’re a fancypants money waster like me, newly introduced EVs are also cheaper than their gas counterparts. You get a faster, nicer car that almost never needs maintenance OR gasoline, and save money.

So why are we even still talking about this antique fuel of a previous era? Why aren’t the candidates also arguing over the price of Kodak film or typewriters or fax machines?

6: The Economy is Something We Should Even Worry About.

The funniest part about all this economic talk is that we’re focusing on the wrong thing. While hard work and business and advancing the frontiers of human knowledge are all fun things, the reality is that we passed the point of having “Enough” decades ago. When the American middle class complains about how hard we have it these days, it’s like a bunch of overfed people at a buffet wishing they could just have one more flavor of donuts stacked onto the table.

According to recent reports, yes, we have income and wealth inequality so that the rich tend to get richer more swiftly. And yes, we should keep that in check with a somewhat progressive tax system because a more equal society tends to be a more peaceful and happy one.

But have you noticed that as the rich people get richer, they don’t get any happier? It’s because after you pass the point of “Enough”, adding more money doesn’t really help much.

In a recent development, and “Enough” is much more defined by your mindset (and your collection of life skills) than your paycheck. So if the politicians really cared about improving our happiness and wellbeing, they’d be preaching the Principles of Mustachianism rather than pandering to the specific requests of coal miners or billionaires.

But alas, winning an election is a very different thing than proposing stuff that is actually best for the country. And for that reason, we cast our votes for the best party and then tune back out until the next election.

In the Comments: Has the election season been getting you down, pumping you up, or just giving you a thorough dose of “Meh”?

Industry observers note that while researching economic stats for this article, I came across a quirky but informative series of videos called USA Facts by none other than former Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer. It seems that he had the same frustration as me: Americans are fighting over a bunch of opinions and misinformation without even bothering to look up the actual facts. So he made a well-produced series of videos that just share the facts without the baggage of political hype on top of them. I wish our politicians could do the same thing!

The Airline Canceled Your Flight – Take the Cash Refund, Not the Voucher

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when an airline cancels or significantly changes your flight within, to, or from the US, it owes you a cash refund of your fare and any extras you paid for.
  • Industry observers note that say the airline cancels your family’s flight at the gate the night before vacation, and the agent offers four travel vouchers.
  • Industry observers note that under a 2024 Department of Transportation rule, any airline flying within, to, or from the US must refund your fare, taxes, and extras like seat fees when it cancels your flight and you turn down its alternatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when an airline cancels or significantly changes your flight within, to, or from the US, it owes you a cash refund of your fare and any extras you paid for. Say no to the voucher and the rebooking unless you want them, because accepting either can cost you that refund.

Industry observers note that say the airline cancels your family’s flight at the gate the night before vacation, and the agent offers four travel vouchers. It feels generous, but the airline is keeping money it already owes you.

Industry observers note that under a 2024 Department of Transportation rule, any airline flying within, to, or from the US must refund your fare, taxes, and extras like seat fees when it cancels your flight and you turn down its alternatives. The refund is automatic, so there’s no claim to file. The reason for the cancellation doesn’t matter, and weather counts.

It has been revealed that A significant change gets you the same refund. That covers any delay or schedule change that moves your departure three or more hours earlier or your arrival three or more hours later (six on international trips). A switch to a different airport, an added connection, or a downgrade to a lower cabin counts too.

Take the rebooking or a voucher only if you want it, because accepting either can end your claim to the refund. If you still need to travel, price a seat yourself before you turn down the rebooking, since a last-minute seat can cost more than the fare you get back. Silence isn’t a yes. If you never answer the offer, the airline has to refund you once the latest flight leaves without you.

Industry observers note that the airline then has seven business days to put the money back on a credit card, or 20 calendar days for a debit card, cash, or check. For your family, that means all four fares, the taxes, and the $120 you paid to sit together. If a travel site charged your card, ask the site for the refund, since agencies owe one only after you request it.

Ask the airline in writing for any money missing at the deadline, and keep a copy. Then file a complaint with the Department of Transportation against an airline that still won’t pay.

Recent findings suggest that when the gate agent offers a voucher, ask for the refund instead. Cash can buy a seat on any airline, while a voucher ties you to the one that just canceled on you.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

In a recent development, picture this: you're reclining in Air France's La Première-adjacent Business cabin somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, a three-course meal on the way, and a fully flat bed waiting for you after dinner. That gap is the entire point. Air France-KLM's Flying Blue program runs what they call **Promo Rewards** — a monthly flash sale on award seats that slashes the points price by 25 to 50% on select routes. In Business class, that can mean seats that would normally cost 80,000+ miles dropping to as low as 40,000 miles one-way. On a route where a cash ticket retails for $3,000, you're extracting **7.5 cents per point** — and on premium routes during peak travel periods, that figure can climb to 15 cents per point. To put that in FI-community terms: the average point is worth 1 to 2 cents when redeemed for cash back or basic travel. This redemption can be worth 6 to 10 times that. If you have 40,000 transferable points sitting in a Chase or Amex account, this is the difference between a $400 economy ticket and a $3,000 business class experience — for the same points. The pricing inefficiency exists because Flying Blue uses these promotional awards as a marketing tool to fill premium cabin seats on specific dates that might otherwise go out with empty seats. Airlines would rather have a loyalist in that seat than fly it empty. You, as someone who's built a transferable points balance, are perfectly positioned to take advantage of the moment they make that trade-off. This isn't a loophole that's about to close. Flying Blue has run Promo Rewards consistently for years. It's a **structural feature of the program** — one the ChooseFI community can build an annual travel strategy around. The challenge isn't finding the deal. It's being ready when it drops.

The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override.

Flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

The Fuel Surcharge Nuance You Must Know.

Flying Blue does pass on carrier-imposed surcharges for standard awards on Air France and KLM flights — this can add $200 to $500 to what should be a points redemption. But here's the critical detail: Promo Reward bookings eliminate those surcharges. You pay the miles, a small booking fee, and that's it. This is a significant hidden value that casual points users miss entirely. The published cash price comparison becomes even more favorable once you factor in that you're not paying the surcharge on top.

The Transfer Path Is Best-in-Class.

Routing Rules Give You Flexibility.

Industry observers note that flying Blue allows open-jaw routing — meaning you can fly into Paris and out of Amsterdam (or vice versa) on a single award, letting you initiative a more dynamic European itinerary without paying for two separate tickets. The booking window opens at 359 days out, and miles are activity-based with a 24-month expiration window, so you're not racing against a clock as long as you keep your account active with occasional small transactions.

Recent findings suggest that getting your phone service and home internet from one manufacturer can cut your combined bill, since phone carriers discount their home internet and cable companies sell low-priced phone lines to their internet customers. Before you switch, add up the bundle’s monthly total and compare it with the cheapest phone plan and internet plan you could buy separately.

The discounts are real, but their conditions decide whether the bundle saves you money.

The substantial phone carriers discount the internet bill:.

Industry observers note that cable companies cut the phone bill instead. Xfinity Mobile’s Mobile Select proposal costs $30 a month per line, and Spectrum Mobile charges $30 a month for each Unlimited line after the first. Both sell only to their own internet customers and run on Verizon’s network.

A bundle is worth it only when its total beats buying both services separately. Add up its monthly cost with every condition met, such as AutoPay and the per-line price for your number of lines. Then price the cheapest phone proposal that covers your data and the cheapest internet plan at your address. Count any money still owed on a phone too, since switching carriers with a balance makes it due.

Say a couple keeps Xfinity Internet and pays a major carrier $110 a month before taxes for two unlimited lines. Two Mobile Select lines cost $60 before taxes, $50 less than the carrier’s $110, though each line’s data can slow when the network is busy once it uses 50GB in a month.

Industry observers note that dropping either service can cost you the discount. T-Mobile’s bill credits stop if you cancel a line, and Xfinity Mobile’s current plans cost $10 a month more for customers who drop Xfinity Internet. Check coverage too, since 5G home internet isn’t sold at every address and a cable company’s phone lines rely on Verizon’s signal where you live and work.

Compare the totals at the prices you’ll pay after the first year, since a free first-year line or a low introductory internet price won’t last.

Who Counts as Your Dependent? A Child or Relative Who Passes the IRS’s Tests

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (503 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Claim someone as your dependent only if they pass every IRS test for a qualifying child or a qualifying relative, tests built on how you’re related, their age and income, where they live, and who supports them.
  • Recent findings suggest that A qualifying child under 17 can bring the child tax credit, and other dependents can bring the credit for other dependents, worth up to $500 each.
  • According to recent reports, A qualifying child can’t pay over half of their own support, but anyone can cover the rest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claim someone as your dependent only if they pass every IRS test for a qualifying child or a qualifying relative, tests built on how you’re related, their age and income, where they live, and who supports them. Check each one before you file, since a dependent can bring tax credits and a better filing status.

Recent findings suggest that A qualifying child under 17 can bring the child tax credit, and other dependents can bring the credit for other dependents, worth up to $500 each. Either kind can also help you file as head of household, usually at lower rates than filing single, or claim the child and dependent care credit.

According to recent reports, A qualifying child can’t pay over half of their own support, but anyone can cover the rest. A qualifying relative must get more than half of their total support from you, though relatives who together pay over half can agree in writing that one who paid over 10% claims them.

In a recent development, A qualifying child is your child, stepchild, foster child, sibling, or stepsibling, or a descendant of one, such as a grandchild. They must live with you over half the year, and temporary absences, like time at school, count as time with you. Unless permanently and totally disabled, they must also be under 19 at year’s end, or 24 if a full-time student.

A qualifying relative must be a relative on the IRS’s list, such as a parent, or live with you all year, and have gross income under a yearly IRS limit.

In a recent development, A parent beats anyone else claiming the same child. If parents on separate returns both claim, the IRS picks the one the child lived with longer, then the one with the higher adjusted gross income (AGI), total income minus certain adjustments. A nonparent can claim a child the parents pass up only with a higher AGI than every parent who could.

According to recent reports, say your widowed mother lives on untaxed Social Security and you pay most of her bills. Those benefits don’t count toward her gross income, but IRS Publication 501 counts what she spends on herself in her total support. If you pay more than half of that total, you can claim her and the credit for other dependents.

Before you file, run each person through the dependent interview in the IRS’s Interactive Tax Assistant. It asks what support you provided, so total what everyone spent on them first.

Latest Update: Retired Man Tries to Spend More Money, Mostly Fails

📅 16 Jan 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1487 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A couple of years ago, Mr.
  • “I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers.
  • Sources indicate that so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

I thought to myself at the time,.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”.

Sources indicate that so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!).

According to recent reports, among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore newly introduced places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

With all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

Industry observers note that while my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the major-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.).

Recent findings suggest that this level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

Sources indicate that as we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a upcoming cost too since I was self-insured back then.

In a recent development, my budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

This strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible plan ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze blueprint in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

In a recent development, but as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which states that,.

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

For me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

It has been revealed that the only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I right now live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out. I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

But I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

But for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?

Will More Money Change You? Automate Giving and Keep Your Old Friends

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (383 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that studies linking wealth to selfishness have a mixed record, so more money won’t necessarily change you.
  • A widely covered 2012 study found drivers of higher-status cars more likely to cut off other cars at a four-way stop and to cut off a pedestrian waiting at a crosswalk.
  • When a study in Austria repeated the crosswalk test with 374 drivers, more than twice the original study’s 152, how expensive a car looked made no measurable difference to whether its driver stopped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that studies linking wealth to selfishness have a mixed record, so more money won’t necessarily change you. To keep it that way, give a set share of your income automatically, keep a regular volunteer shift, and keep seeing the friends you had before the money.

A widely covered 2012 study found drivers of higher-status cars more likely to cut off other cars at a four-way stop and to cut off a pedestrian waiting at a crosswalk. In lab tests, its upper-class participants were also more likely to lie in a negotiation and cheat to win a prize.

Later tests have had mixed results. When a study in Austria repeated the crosswalk test with 374 drivers, more than twice the original study’s 152, how expensive a car looked made no measurable difference to whether its driver stopped. And in a Dutch experiment published in 2021, wealthy households returned 81% of letters delivered to them by mistake, against 38% for households with little wealth.

Recent findings suggest that research on paying people for help is shaky too. In Heyman and Ariely’s 2004 experiments, people sometimes worked harder for nothing than for a small payment. The journal has since flagged the paper with an expression of concern, citing statistics that didn’t match a recalculation. Two repeats of one of its studies, run with 3,302 people in all and published in 2022, backed only part of that study’s findings.

Three habits help keep you generous whichever way the research settles.

Three signs mean a habit is slipping: putting a price on every favor, seeing less of old friends, and feeling exempt from rules everyone else follows.

Set up the recurring gift in the first month of your higher income, through the charity’s website or a paycheck deduction at work.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the last few years before you retire, move the money you’ll spend in your first five to 10 years of retirement into low-risk holdings, such as Treasuries, certificates of deposit (CDs), and high-quality bond funds.
  • A stock market drop does the most damage in the first years after you retire, when you’d have to sell shares at low prices to pay the bills.
  • Whether a dollar needs protecting depends on when you’ll spend it, not on how old you are.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the last few years before you retire, move the money you’ll spend in your first five to 10 years of retirement into low-risk holdings, such as Treasuries, certificates of deposit (CDs), and high-quality bond funds. Size the amount by years of planned withdrawals, not by your age, and leave the rest invested.

A stock market drop does the most damage in the first years after you retire, when you’d have to sell shares at low prices to pay the bills. That danger, called sequence of returns risk, is why the money you’ll spend first shouldn’t stay in stocks.

Whether a dollar needs protecting depends on when you’ll spend it, not on how old you are. Money in stocks that you’ll need within 10 years may not have time to recover from a crash, while money you won’t touch for a decade or more can stay there and ride out a slump.

Each of these holds up far better than stocks in a crash, and each comes with a catch.

Holdings bought for their income can still fall in the same crash that hits your stocks. In 2008, when the S&P 500 lost 36.55% with dividends counted, 10-year Treasuries gained 20.10%, according to NYU professor Aswath Damodaran’s historical returns data.

According to recent reports, size the safe money by your withdrawals. Add up what you’ll take from savings each year beyond Social Security and any pension, then multiply by the five to 10 years you want covered. A rule based on age alone, like holding a bond percentage equal to your age, ignores what you’ll actually spend.

It has been revealed that an emergency fund and cash for other goals don’t count toward it. Those belong in safe places to earn interest, matched to when you’ll need them.

According to recent reports, say you’re 60, plan to retire at 63, and will need $40,000 a year from savings. Over the next three years, you’d build a five-year ladder of Treasuries and CDs worth $200,000, with $40,000 coming due each year from 63 through 67, and leave the rest invested. These figures are only an illustration, so run the math with your own.

About three years before your retirement date, start moving the money for those years of withdrawals into these holdings, the first year’s money first, and finish before your last paycheck.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

#159735. Industry News: Pay Less for a Healthier Lawn – Mow High, Water Deeply, and Leave the Clippings

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (489 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Pay Less for a Healthier Lawn – Mow High, Water Deeply, and Leave the Clippings

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (489 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, spend less on lawn care by mowing at the top of your grass’s recommended height, leaving the clippings where they fall, and watering deeply once or twice a week instead of daily.
  • Mowing short and watering a little every day both keep grass roots shallow, so the lawn dries out faster, lets more weeds sprout, and costs more to keep green.
  • Industry observers note that grass kept tall grows longer roots that handle drought better, and its shade keeps weed seeds from sprouting, University of Minnesota Extension notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, spend less on lawn care by mowing at the top of your grass’s recommended height, leaving the clippings where they fall, and watering deeply once or twice a week instead of daily. A lawn kept that way needs less water and fertilizer, and the work is simple enough to do yourself.

Mowing short and watering a little every day both keep grass roots shallow, so the lawn dries out faster, lets more weeds sprout, and costs more to keep green.

Industry observers note that grass kept tall grows longer roots that handle drought better, and its shade keeps weed seeds from sprouting, University of Minnesota Extension notes. Virginia Tech’s extension service says deep, infrequent soakings keep the root system healthy too.

Clippings left on the lawn feed it about as much as one fertilizer application a year.

Mow at the top of your grass type’s recommended height, 3 inches or more for most Midwest lawns, and never cut more than a third of the blade at once. Water about an inch a week, rain included, in one or two soakings, or three on the sandiest soils. Do it early in the morning, when the least water is lost to evaporation and wind. Where grass keeps thinning, reseed with a grass suited to your region, or replace that patch with mulch, ground cover, or native plants that need no mowing.

Feed the lawn once or twice a year instead of a four-step program’s four rounds. The main feeding goes in September for cool-weather grasses like fescue and in late May or early June for warm-weather ones like zoysia, though bermudagrass needs more feedings. To loosen packed soil, split a core aerator rental with a neighbor. Angi puts a day’s rental at $80 to $120, or $40 to $60 each plus your labor, against $75 to $250 to hire a pro.

In a recent development, angi’s mower price guide puts a weekly mowing service at about $45 a visit on average, so a season of visits from May through October costs about $1,170. Buying a $240 electric push mower, Angi’s average, and mowing yourself instead of paying that $1,170 leaves you about $930 ahead the first year, before charging, tune-ups, and your time.

Before your next mow, raise the cutting height. Then set five empty tuna cans across your sprinkler’s reach, time how long they take to collect an inch, and water that long each week.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

Latest Update: Eat the Same Produce for Less – Skip the Precut Packs and Buy Frozen Off-Season

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (328 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that to spend less on fruits and vegetables without eating fewer of them, buy them whole instead of precut and switch to frozen or canned when fresh is out of season.
  • In a recent development, in the USDA’s fruit and vegetable price data for 2023, cauliflower cut from a whole head averaged 66 cents per cup you’d eat, against $1.13 for precut florets.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that to spend less on fruits and vegetables without eating fewer of them, buy them whole instead of precut and switch to frozen or canned when fresh is out of season. Blueprint meals around your store’s weekly produce sale, and buy only the fresh produce your family will eat before it spoils.

In a recent development, in the USDA’s fruit and vegetable price data for 2023, cauliflower cut from a whole head averaged 66 cents per cup you’d eat, against $1.13 for precut florets. Celery from a bunch you trim yourself averaged 48 cents a cup, against 70 cents for sticks.

Fresh prices also change with the season. Strawberries averaged $2.22 for a 12-ounce pack in July 2025 and $3.61 in December, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. In the same USDA data, frozen blueberries averaged $1.39 a cup, against $1.73 fresh, and canned green beans 54 cents, against 87 cents fresh.

Frozen keeps its vitamins, too. A University of Georgia study found no real difference in vitamin content between frozen and fresh produce in most of its comparisons.

So buy each fruit or vegetable in whatever form costs least when you shop.

At the USDA’s 2023 prices, a family eating 4 cups a week each of cauliflower, celery, and blueberries saves about $4 a week by buying the first two whole and the berries frozen instead of precut and fresh. That comes to more than $200 a year.

#159728. 23 Ways to Save Money on Vacation – Plan, Book, and Spend for Less

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2449 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Moneycrashers ↗ Open Full Page

23 Ways to Save Money on Vacation – Plan, Book, and Spend for Less

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2449 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Save the most on a vacation by deciding when to go, how to fly, and where to sleep before you book anything, since those choices set the trip’s biggest costs.
  • scheduled passenger airlines collected $7.4 billion in baggage fees in 2025, the Bureau of Transportation Statistics reports, and a bag fee is one charge you can often skip.
  • The moves below are grouped by when you’d make them: while planning the trip, while booking it, and once you’re on your way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Save the most on a vacation by deciding when to go, how to fly, and where to sleep before you book anything, since those choices set the trip’s biggest costs. Then trim the remaining costs with smaller moves at the airport and once you arrive.

U.S. scheduled passenger airlines collected $7.4 billion in baggage fees in 2025, the Bureau of Transportation Statistics reports, and a bag fee is one charge you can often skip.

The moves below are grouped by when you’d make them: while planning the trip, while booking it, and once you’re on your way. The money they save can go back into the trip itself, so spending less doesn’t have to mean seeing less.

Paying for the trip from savings means no credit card balance after you’re home, and every other move on this list shrinks the amount you need to save.

In a recent development, price your next vacation, divide the cost by the months until you leave, and set up an automatic transfer for that amount into a high-yield savings account used only for the trip. Send windfalls like a tax refund or a work bonus there too, to reach the full cost sooner.

Read more: Pay for Your Next Vacation Before You Go - Automate Savings Into Its Own Account.

Where you go sets the price of the flight and much of the rest of the trip, so it pays to keep your options open if more than one place would make you happy.

Industry observers note that pick your vacation spot first, and you pay whatever it costs to fly there. Instead, search a fare map from your home airport with the destination left blank. Set price alerts on a short list of trips you’d happily take, and book when one drops to a price you’re willing to pay.

Read more: Let the Deals Pick Your Destination - Start With What's Cheap From Your Airport.

Flights and rooms at popular places cost the most when everyone wants to go, so travelers who know where they’re headed but can be flexible about dates stand to save.

Move your trip into the destination’s shoulder season, the weeks just before or after its peak, and the same flights often cost less, with thinner crowds and weather that’s usually still good. The discount varies by place and year, so compare prices for several weeks around your dates before you book.

Read more: Travel in the Shoulder Season - Price the Same Trip Week by Week.

On a short trip to a big city, the room’s location, how you get around, and which sights you pay for decide much of what you spend.

It has been revealed that on a city weekend, book a room near a train line rather than downtown, ride transit instead of paying to park, and blueprint your days around sights that are free for visitors. Buy an attractions pass only if the places you’ll see would cost more at the gate.

Read more: A Cheaper City Weekend - Stay Near a Train Line and Do the Pass Math.

Even with the place and the week settled, the fare for the same route can change with the day you fly and the airport you leave from.

The cheapest flight usually goes to the traveler who can shift dates or airports. Search a calendar of fares instead of fixed dates, include every airport near you, and set a price alert so you can book when the fare dips. Compare fares only after adding the bags and seat you’ll pay for.

Read more: Find the Cheapest Flight - Search Flexible Dates & Nearby Airports, Then Track the Price.

Credit card points you’ve already collected can pay for the flight instead of cash, which leaves more of the trip’s budget for everything else.

Flexible credit card points can usually move into an airline’s frequent flyer program at one point per mile. There, the same flight often costs far fewer points than in your card’s travel portal, plus taxes and fees in cash. Find the seat on the airline’s site first, then transfer only what the booking needs, since transfers are final.

Read more: Transfer Card Points to Airline Partners - Same Flight, Often Far Fewer Points.

Bag fees come on top of the fare and repeat on every flight, so frequent flyers and families have the most to gain here.

Carry on whenever your fare includes a carry-on bag, since a checked bag now costs $45 or more each way on Delta, American, and Southwest. If you check bags on most trips, get an airline credit card or elite status that waives the first bag for you and the companions on your reservation.

Read more: Avoid Checked Bag Fees - Carry On, or Get Them Waived for Your Whole Party.

Solo travelers and couples who would rather spend on the destination than on hotel extras are the ones a hostel suits best.

According to recent reports, many hostels rent private rooms, not just dorm bunks, for well under a hotel room’s price, though you may share a bathroom. Book one that recent guests rate highly for security and location, and cook in the shared kitchen to cut your food bill too.

Read more: Book a Hostel's Private Room for About 40% Less Than a Hotel - Bunks Optional.

If the trip is about hiking or scenery, a campsite puts you inside the park itself, with no hotel bill at all.

A campsite in a state or national park costs a fraction of a hotel room, but popular campgrounds can fill the day reservations open. Book on Recreation.gov or your state’s park reservation site that morning, buy an annual pass if you’ll visit several parks, and borrow gear for your first trip.

Read more: Park Campsites Cost a Fraction of a Hotel Room - Book the Day Reservations Open.

House-sitting takes more groundwork than booking a room, so it suits travelers with flexible dates who like animals and plan to travel this way more than once.

House-sitting gets you a free place to stay in exchange for caring for someone’s home and pets while they’re away. Join a house-sitting site and earn your first reviews on short sits near home, since owners choose sitters by their reviews. Then apply for longer sits whose dates and pets fit you.

Read more: House-Sit for Free Lodging - Earn Reviews Near Home Before You Sit Abroad.

Restaurant meals for a family get expensive over a long stay, so the room you pick can decide how much of the food budget goes to eating out.

For a family trip of three nights or more, compare a hotel suite, extended-stay room, or rental with a kitchen to a standard room. Add up the kitchen’s extra cost for the whole stay, any cleaning fee included, and book the one with the kitchen if cooking breakfast and a few dinners would save your family more than that.

Read more: Book a Room With a Kitchen - Cooking Breakfast Can Cover the Higher Rate.

When cooking isn’t an option, a free hotel breakfast can still take one meal a day off the family’s food bill.

Industry observers note that midprice hotel chains such as Hampton by Hilton, Holiday Inn Express, and Drury include a hot breakfast in the room rate. When you compare hotels, add what your family would spend on breakfast out to the cheaper room’s rate, and book the breakfast hotel when its rate is lower than that total.

Read more: 12 Hotel Chains With Free Breakfast - and When They Beat a Cheaper Room.

Travelers who’ve already picked a chain hotel can still get more for their money, and this check takes only a few minutes before you book.

Before you book a chain hotel through a booking app, check the chain’s own site, signed in to its free loyalty program. Members often pay no more there than on the app, and booking through the app forfeits the chain’s points and credit toward elite status. Compare the same room, dates, and cancellation terms at the final price.

Read more: The Hotel's Member Rate Often Beats the Booking App - Check It Before You Book.

The discount comes from something you already belong to, so checking costs nothing, and it applies to cruises as well as hotels.

Before you book a hotel or cruise, check the member rates you already have through a warehouse club, AAA or AARP, your employer, your credit union, or military service. Price the same trip booked direct too, subtract any shop card or onboard credit the member deal adds, and book whichever costs less.

Read more: Your Memberships Can Cut Hotel & Cruise Prices - Check Each Against Booking Direct.

This move can still save money after you’ve booked, so it suits travelers who reserve a hotel early to be sure of a room.

Sources indicate that A refundable hotel rate usually costs more than a prepaid one, but it lets you rebook the same room for less if the price drops before your stay. Book one early, set a price alert for your dates, and when the rate falls, reserve the cheaper room first and cancel the original second.

Read more: A Refundable Hotel Booking Can Only Get Cheaper - Rebook When Prices Drop.

Prepaying for flights and rooms saves money until something cancels the trip, and buying a travel insurance policy you don’t need would undo part of those savings.

Many credit cards repay prepaid, nonrefundable costs when illness, severe weather, or another covered reason cancels or cuts short a trip you paid for with the card, and some cover meals and lodging during a long delay. Check your card’s guide to benefits before you buy travel insurance, and book with a card that carries the coverage.

Read more: Your Credit Card Can Cover a Canceled Trip - Check It Before Buying Travel Insurance.

Airport restaurants and shops charge more than the same food costs at home, and the gap grows on a long travel day or with a family to feed.

Pack sandwiches and snacks from your kitchen and carry an empty water bottle to fill past security, since TSA lets solid food and empty bottles through the checkpoint. Spreads, yogurt, and drinks fall under the liquids rule, so each needs a container of 3.4 ounces or less.

Read more: Airport Food Is Optional - TSA Lets You Bring Lunch and an Empty Water Bottle.

Unlike most moves here, this one pays you instead of cutting a cost, which suits travelers with nothing urgent waiting at their destination.

It has been revealed that if you can arrive a few hours late, volunteer your seat when an airline oversells your flight, and treat its first offer as an opening bid. Before you accept, get a confirmed seat on a later flight and ask what the travel credit is worth, when it expires, and whether you can take cash instead.

Read more: Volunteer Your Seat on an Oversold Flight - Then Negotiate Before You Accept.

Rental companies offer extra coverage at pickup, charged by the day, so its cost grows with every day of a road trip.

Check whether your credit card covers collision damage and theft on rental cars before your next trip. Many cards do, but only if you pay for the whole rental with that card and decline the counter’s damage waiver. Read your card’s benefits guide first to confirm the coverage, then skip the waiver’s daily charge.

Read more: Decline the Rental Counter's Damage Waiver If Your Credit Card Covers the Car.

International travelers can sort this out at home, before the trip, and a fee-free card used to pay in the local currency avoids both a card fee and a currency markup.

Sources indicate that before you travel abroad, check your credit card for a foreign transaction fee, usually 1% to 3% of every purchase processed outside the U.S. If it has one, pack a card that charges none. The fee buys you nothing, and it adds up over a whole trip.

Read more: Pack a Card With No Foreign Transaction Fee - Others Charge Up to 3%.

Abroad, the offer to pay in dollars appears at checkout after checkout, so it helps to know your answer before you’re first asked.

It has been revealed that when a card terminal, ATM, or foreign website offers to charge you in U.S. dollars, decline and pay in the local currency. Saying yes lets the merchant or ATM operator set the exchange rate, and its markup routinely adds several percent to what your own card would charge.

Read more: Choose the Local Currency Abroad - The Dollar Option Comes With a Markup.

Some places abroad take only cash, such as small shops, markets, and taxis, so most international travelers need some local money on hand.

According to recent reports, before a trip abroad, get a debit card that charges no foreign transaction or ATM fees. When you arrive, use it to take out local cash at a bank’s ATM, and pick the local currency over dollars when the screen asks. That withdrawal costs less than changing money at a counter or taking a credit card cash advance.

Read more: Get Cash Abroad at a Bank's ATM - On a Debit Card Without Foreign Fees.

Maps, translation, and ride-hailing apps all use data, so most travelers abroad need some, and how you buy it sets the price.

Before you take your phone abroad, check whether your initiative already includes data where you’re going. If it doesn’t, download a travel eSIM from an app, since a week of its data can cost less than two days of Verizon’s or AT&T’s $12 day pass. Turn off data roaming on your U.S. line before you land.

Read more: Phone Data Abroad - A Travel eSIM Costs a Fraction of a Carrier's Day Pass.

Sources indicate that pair a receipt scanning app that pays per receipt, Fetch for gift cards or Receipt Hog for PayPal cash, with one that pays per featured product, Ibotta or Checkout 51, and use both on every grocery trip. Expect a few dollars a month from your receipts, since one with no bonus earns cents.

It has been revealed that fetch pays at least 25 points for any paper receipt and values 1,000 points at roughly $1 in gift cards, so a receipt with no bonus works out to about 2.5 cents. Most of its rewards start at 3,000 points, and your first has to be $10 or more.

Industry observers note that every app here pays on the receipts you already bring home. Some pay a little for each receipt, and others pay cash back only for what their offers feature, mostly specific products. In return, each app shares data on what you buy with brands or other business partners. Amazon also pays up to $10 a month in Amazon credit for other stores’ receipts, though space on its shopper panel is limited. Other savings need no receipt photo at all, such as card-linked offers you add to the card you pay with and your store app’s digital coupons.

Receipts from restaurants, gas stations, and malls earn its 25-point minimum too, though three receipts a week with no bonus come to about 325 points a month, roughly 33 cents by our math.

For more information, read our full Fetch Review.

Pick it over Fetch if you’d rather have PayPal cash than gift cards, or snap your grocery receipts into both, since nothing in either app’s terms bars it.

For more information, read our full Receipt Hog Review.

At Walmart, CVS, and Dollar General, a linked store account used at checkout pays the offers you added before shopping with nothing to snap, so those receipts go only into your per-receipt app.

For more information, read our full Ibotta Review.

Its gas offers pay only if no other cash back program pays on the same fill-up, so give gas receipts to Checkout 51 alone and grocery receipts to it and your per-receipt app.

For more information, read our full Checkout 51 Review.

Receipt apps pay small amounts, so what you earn depends on snapping every receipt, week after week, into apps that fit how you shop. Start with one that pays per receipt in the form you’d rather be paid, gift cards or PayPal cash, and pair it with an app whose featured brands you already buy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that before you buy sports tickets, price the same section at the team’s box office, on its official resale site, and on two or three ticket marketplaces, comparing the totals each indicates with fees included. Then buy only where a guarantee covers a fake ticket or a canceled game.

Industry observers note that comparing those totals got easier on May 12, 2025, when the Federal Trade Commission’s Rule on Unfair or Deceptive Fees took effect. It requires any business that advertises or lists live-event tickets, resale sites included, to show the total price up front, including mandatory fees.

Only taxes, delivery charges, and extras you choose to add can wait until checkout, so the first price you see is close to what you’ll pay. The totals still differ for seats in the same section, though. Each seller charges its own fees, and resale tickets are priced by whoever lists them. That price can be above face value, the base price the team sets, or below it.

Industry observers note that the guarantee is the other half of the comparison. The major marketplaces all promise valid tickets that arrive in time, but they differ on postponed games, on refunds versus credit, and on whether you get replacement seats.

Start with the team, since a ticket it sells you is genuine.

Recent findings suggest that buying straight from another fan skips the fees and, usually, any guarantee. With a mobile ticket, have the seller transfer it to your account and accept it before you pay. On Ticketmaster, accepting a transfer challenges you a new barcode only you can use, and the seller’s copy stops working.

U.S. PIRG notes that the federal Fair Credit Billing Act gives credit card buyers far stronger protection than debit card buyers against fake tickets. So buy the lowest total that comes with a guarantee, and pay for it with a credit card.

One of the highest-value redemptions in travel rewards.

Industry observers note that picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok. Two bucket-list cities. One award booking. One points balance. This is what the Aeroplan stopover sweet spot feels like in practice. It's not a trick or a loophole — it's a deliberately designed feature of Air Canada's Aeroplan program that the vast majority of travelers simply don't know exists. And that gap between awareness and reality is exactly where the ChooseFI community finds its edge. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. That's a realistic retail range depending on season and how far out you book. Most people never consider it a possibility for a family vacation or a milestone trip because the sticker price puts it in a different universe. With Aeroplan, you're booking that same itinerary — the same seats, the same lounges, the same Turkish Airlines or Thai Airways product — for **75,000 Aeroplan points**. At the low end of the cash price range, that's already **8 cents per point**. At the high end, you're extracting **20 cents per point** from a currency that most people earned by putting groceries on a credit card. The pricing inefficiency here is structural. Aeroplan's partner award chart prices long-haul business class at a fixed rate regardless of cash fare fluctuations. When business class prices spike — around holidays, during peak travel seasons, during major events — your points cost stays exactly the same. You're insulated from the market. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: you've already paid for the trip in points, slowly accumulated through everyday spending, and now you're simply redeeming the stored value. The stopover itself is nearly free. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 extra miles to add a stopover city to a one-way award. That means your Istanbul layover becomes a multi-day stay — at zero additional points cost beyond that small add-on — and you haven't booked a second award at all. One booking. Two destinations. That's the entire premise, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

When Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. This is critical. When you book Turkish Airlines business class through Aeroplan, you pay the Aeroplan fixed chart rate — not what Turkish Airlines would charge in its own currency or miles program, and not the inflated cash price. That fixed chart is the engine of this redemption.

For long-haul international business class, Aeroplan's chart prices routing through multiple regions based on your origin and destination — not every intermediate stop. This is the aha moment. Aeroplan determines your award price based on where your journey starts and where it ends, and then allows you to add a stopover in between for just 5,000 additional miles. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

Industry observers note that on a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

According to recent reports, the routing must be geographically sensible — you can't fly backwards across the globe — but Aeroplan's allowance for multi-segment itineraries through Star Alliance hubs gives you enormous flexibility. Istanbul (IST) is a Turkish Airlines hub. Bangkok (BKK) is served by Thai Airways and several Star Alliance carriers. Both are Star Alliance partners. Both are bookable through Aeroplan at fixed chart rates with no fuel surcharges.

Having Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency means you can search, find space, and transfer points before the availability window closes. The 1:1 ratio across all four programs means no conversion math — every point you earn translates directly to one Aeroplan mile.

According to recent reports, booking an Aeroplan stopover award in business class is genuinely one of the more complex redemptions in the travel rewards world, but it becomes manageable when you break it into distinct phases. Here's exactly how to do it.

It has been revealed that start by deciding on your two destinations. Aeroplan stopovers work best when your intermediate city is a major Star Alliance hub that lies geographically between your origin and final destination. Classic combinations include North America to Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub) continuing to Southeast Asia, or North America to a European hub continuing to the Middle East or East Africa. Your stopover city should be somewhere you genuinely want to spend 2–5 days — this is a real trip, not just a layover.

Sources indicate that this is the most key and most time-consuming step. You need to find saver-level business class availability on both segments independently before you book.

Once you've confirmed availability on both segments, go to aeroplan.com and use the multi-city search function. Enter your full itinerary — origin, stopover city with your intended layover dates, and final destination.

Once you've confirmed the award is bookable and are ready to complete the reservation:.

Complete your booking on aeroplan.com or with a phone agent, confirm the stopover is properly reflected in your itinerary, and save every confirmation email. Verify your seats on each carrier's website immediately after booking.

A stopover is an intentional break in your journey lasting more than 24 hours at a connecting city. Most airlines treat stopovers as separate tickets, charging full price for each segment. Aeroplan is one of the few programs that allows a free stopover on round-trip awards, letting you explore a connecting city for days before continuing to your final destination. This is fundamentally different from a layover, which is a brief connection of a few hours at an airport. The stopover must be in a city served by a Star Alliance carrier on your routing, and the key is that Aeroplan prices the entire itinerary as one award, not two.

The Route: Toronto (YYZ) → Istanbul (IST, 4-day stopover) → Bangkok (BKK) The Carrier: Turkish Airlines business class on both segments The Points Cost: 75,000 Aeroplan miles for the two segments + 5,000 miles for the stopover = 80,000 Aeroplan miles total Cash Equivalent: A comparable business class itinerary on this routing typically retails for $9,000–$12,000 in 2026, depending on when you search and how far in advance you book.

The Turkish Airlines business class product on long-haul routes is consistently rated among the top business class experiences in the Star Alliance network. On the YYZ–IST segment — operated on a 787 or A330 — you'll have access to a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, the Turkish Airlines Lounge in Istanbul (widely considered one of the best airport lounges in the world, full stop), and a meal service that reflects the airline's culinary reputation. The IST lounge alone — with its restaurant, spa, golf simulator, and sleeping areas — is worth lingering in even before your onward connection.

According to recent reports, in Istanbul, your four days might include the Hagia Sophia at sunrise, a Bosphorus dinner cruise, and the Grand Bazaar before you head to the airport to continue your journey. You've paid nothing additional for this stay beyond the 5,000-mile stopover fee.

The IST–BKK segment puts you into Bangkok in the evening, ready for Thailand's extraordinary food, culture, and cost of living — which, for the FI-minded traveler, means your lodging and meals on the ground are remarkably affordable, stretching the value of your trip even further.

Total points cost for two lie-flat business class segments and a full European city stay: 80,000 miles, earned on everyday credit card spending. That's the entire proposition, and those numbers are real.

Book at exactly 355 days out. Aeroplan opens its booking window at 355 days before departure. The best business class availability on popular routes — especially Turkish Airlines long-haul — appears at this window and gets claimed quickly. Set a calendar reminder and be ready to search at the 355-day mark for your target travel dates.

In a recent development, use Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency for this redemption. The instant transfer speed to Aeroplan is genuinely differentiating. When you find award space and need to move swiftly, Chase lets you transfer and book in the same session. Amex, Capital One, and Bilt all require 1–2 days, during which your availability can evaporate.

Search availability before you transfer points. Confirm space exists on every segment before a single point moves. There's no undo button on a transfer, and Aeroplan points sitting idle in your account are fine — points transferred to an account where you can't find availability are a headache.

Call Aeroplan for complex routings. The online multi-city tool is functional but can struggle with nuanced stopover configurations. Phone agents are experienced with these bookings and have the same access to inventory. The call is worth it for an $80,000-point booking.

Industry observers note that leverage the open-jaw rule too. Aeroplan also allows open-jaw routing — fly into one city, depart from another. Combined with the stopover, you can design a route that visits three geographic points on a single award: fly into Istanbul, take trains or ferries to Athens, and fly home from Athens. The award prices the same way.

Don't assume partner availability matches Aeroplan's search. Turkish Airlines and other Star Alliance partners don't always make every seat available through Aeroplan's online portal. If you see space on the carrier's own site but not on aeroplan.com, call — agents can often access inventory the website misses.

Don't book inflexible connecting flights. Long-haul itineraries with tight connections are a risk. Build in at least a 3-hour connection at hub airports to protect against irregular operations that could affect your award segments.

Don't earn Marriott Bonvoy® points with this redemption in mind. The 3:1 transfer ratio to Aeroplan makes Marriott a poor choice for funding this specific award. Stick to Amex, Chase, Capital One, or Bilt at 1:1.

Don't book this for a time-sensitive trip. Award availability, transfer timelines, and multi-carrier coordination mean this requires planning runway. Build in at least 3–4 weeks of lead time beyond the actual booking date.

This redemption is purpose-built for the advanced travel rewards enthusiast in the ChooseFI community — someone who has already mastered the basics (earning transferable points, understanding award charts, booking straightforward partner awards) and is ready to unlock the next level of value.

Industry observers note that the ideal profile: A couple or solo traveler planning a milestone trip — a significant anniversary, a sabbatical, a once-in-a-decade adventure — who wants to experience two destinations in business class without paying business class prices for either one. You're flexible on travel dates, comfortable spending time on the phone with an airline agent, and genuinely excited about the trip-planning process as part of the experience.

Pick a final destination and a stopover city on the same Star Alliance routing. Classic combos: Istanbul + Bangkok, Zurich + Tokyo, Vienna + Singapore. The stopover city must be a natural connection point on a Star Alliance route between your origin and destination.

Set a calendar alert for 355 days before your departure date. Search for business class availability on each segment separately using United.com or Aeroplan.com. Both legs need saver-level award space on the same booking.

Before transferring any points, verify that saver award space exists on both the outbound leg (origin to stopover city) and the continuation (stopover city to final destination). If either segment is unavailable, the booking will not work.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant) or Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days) to your Aeroplan account at a 1:1 ratio. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability on both segments.

Call Aeroplan or use the multi-city search tool online. Specify your stopover city and duration (up to the maximum allowed). The system prices it as one round-trip award. Confirm total points match expectations before completing the booking.

Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on round-trip awards. You can stay in your stopover city for a few days or several weeks, giving you genuine time to explore rather than just passing through.

No, stopovers are only available on round-trip awards through Aeroplan. One-way bookings do not qualify for the free stopover benefit. This is one reason round-trip awards can offer better value than two one-ways.

Industry observers note that aeroplan has improved its online multi-city search tool, and some stopover itineraries can now be booked online. However, complex routings may still require a phone call. When calling, clearly state you want a round-trip award with a stopover and specify your stopover city and dates.

Recent findings suggest that the best stopover cities are Star Alliance hub cities with strong business class availability: Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Zurich (SWISS hub), Vienna (Austrian hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), and Tokyo (ANA hub). These hubs offer the most consistent saver-level award space.

The Aeroplan stopover is one of the most powerful tools in the travel rewards playbook. By adding a free stopover to a round-trip business class award, you can explore two world-class cities for the points cost of visiting one. It requires planning, patience at the 355-day booking window, and comfort with Star Alliance routing rules, but the payoff is extraordinary: 10-15 cents per point in value on experiences that would cost thousands in cash. For the FI community member who has mastered basic award bookings and is ready to level up, this is the redemption that changes how you think about travel.
